title: Umar at Jerusalem
hook: Umar receives Jerusalem's surrender, and tradition says he prayed outside the church so it would stay a church

segments.voice: Yesterday: the diwan, and a crying baby that changed a rule. Your line was a share for every child.

It's time to pray, and the leader of the believers is standing inside a church. Not just any church: the great church in Jerusalem that Christians built over the place where they remember Christ's tomb. The city has just surrendered. The patriarch who handed it over is beside him. And Umar, the story goes, is asked to pray right there, inside. He says no. Today: Umar at Jerusalem, and why, as the story is told, he stepped outside.
screen: `TIME TO PRAY, INSIDE A CHURCH.` → `THE CITY HAS SURRENDERED.` → `UMAR SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The Qur'an and hadith don't tell this story. It comes from later chroniclers, one of them a Christian patriarch of Alexandria, and Muslims and Christians have both retold it. It is tradition, not scripture. Jerusalem's patriarch, Sophronius, agreed to surrender the city, but only to the caliph himself. So Umar came. The histories preserve a covenant of safety for the people of the city, which in its usual form promises them their lives, their property and their churches: the churches would not be lived in, torn down or reduced. The versions of that document differ, and scholars debate its wording. Then the story. While Umar was being shown the Church of the Resurrection, the time of prayer came. The patriarch invited him to pray where he stood. Umar declined. If I pray here, he is reported to have said, the Muslims after me will take it, saying: Umar prayed here. So he went out and prayed on the steps outside, alone. Tradition places a mosque named for him near that spot, and the church still stands as a church. The man with every power to take the building chose a smaller thing: to protect it from his own followers' devotion to him. He knew his prayer would become a claim. The Qur'an itself names cloisters, churches, synagogues and mosques together as places where God's name is remembered much, places it says would have been pulled down if God did not check one people by another.
screen: `A STORY FROM LATER CHRONICLERS.` · `A COVENANT FOR THE CHURCHES.` · `IF I PRAY HERE, THEY WILL TAKE IT.` · `HE PRAYED ON THE STEPS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HE PRAYED OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place that's holy to someone else: a church, a temple, a synagogue, a gurdwara, a grave, a corner of a friend's home where they pray. Picture yourself at its door, and ask what it would mean to honor it on its own terms: shoes off, a lowered voice, no photo.
Al-Quds, the holy, Jerusalem's Arabic name: the city where Umar, the caliph, received its surrender and stepped outside a church to pray so it would stay a church. Today's word.
Your line: he prayed outside. So a church could stay a church. That's day eight hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 873 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: JUSTICE FOR A COPTIC BOY.`

notes: The prayer-outside story is attributed to later chroniclers, chiefly Eutychius (Sa'id ibn Batriq, Melkite patriarch of Alexandria); confirm the attribution and 'a Christian bishop of Alexandria'.

The covenant ('Umariyya) is summarized in its commonly cited form (lives, property, churches not inhabited, destroyed or reduced). Tabari's version also contains a clause about Jews, omitted here; versions differ. A Keeper and a historian should confirm the summary is fair.
Sophronius as patriarch and his insistence on surrendering to the caliph in person: from the histories; confirm.
The Mosque of Umar near the Church of the Holy Sepulchre: stated as tradition says; confirm.
Qur'an 22:40 paraphrased; Pickthall's wording uses 'oratories' where this paraphrase says synagogues. Confirm.
Christian perspectives on the surrender are mentioned only as Christians retelling the story; no ranking.
Editor pass: Sophronius and Eutychius called patriarch, not bishop, consistently; mosque line reworded; varied 'turn it over'.

Audit pass: cut repeated framing ('hold it as tradition. Here's how it goes', used again on 874); varied the practice opener. Eutychius places Umar's prayer on the steps at the church door and adds a written ruling that Muslims pray there only singly; the script's summary is consistent with that.
